title: Logical Processing of a Query
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of logical processing of a query.
Apply conceptual processing order in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.
Validate the result against the expected behavior and identify one portability, safety, or edge-case consideration.

content.intro: Learn logical processing of a query through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Logical Processing of a Query matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: The practical goal of logical processing of a query is to produce a result set whose meaning is clear. Confirm which rows enter the query, how values are transformed or combined, and whether NULLs, duplicates, ties, or one-to-many relationships change the output.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Conceptual processing order, FROM and join processing, WHERE filtering, Grouping and HAVING. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Conceptual processing order
items.text: Conceptual processing order helps you read and shape result sets with SELECT, expressions, aliases, sorting, filtering, limits, pagination, and careful NULL reasoning. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: FROM and join processing
items.text: FROM and join processing determines how rows from related sources are matched. Write the join predicate explicitly and check whether multiple matches can multiply rows; use a LEFT JOIN when unmatched left-side records must remain visible.

items.title: WHERE filtering
items.text: WHERE filtering helps you read and shape result sets with SELECT, expressions, aliases, sorting, filtering, limits, pagination, and careful NULL reasoning. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Grouping and HAVING
items.text: Grouping and HAVING summarizes rows. Decide the grain of the result first, group only by the dimensions that define one output row, and verify NULL and duplicate behavior in each metric.

content_blocks.code:
SELECT product_id, name, price
FROM products
WHERE price >= 25 AND is_active = TRUE
ORDER BY price DESC, product_id;
content_blocks.expected_output: The query filters active products at or above the chosen price threshold, then sorts the remaining rows.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in a disposable local PostgreSQL database such as codeleaf_sql_lab after loading datasets/postgresql-lab-setup.sql. Do not use production credentials or a production database. Some specialist examples require optional extensions or a specific PostgreSQL version, as stated in the lesson. The CodeLeaf lesson Run button in this scaffold only previews the documented expected output; it is not a SQL execution service.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

content.task: Try it yourself: demonstrate logical processing of a query using the sample schema. State what each returned row represents, test one edge case related to the lesson, and record the result.
task_acceptance_criteria: The query or design example matches the lesson's intended behavior.
The expected row grain and relevant NULL, duplicate, boundary, or permission behavior are explained.
The test is performed only in the local disposable lab, or clearly marked as a static inspection when a real runner is unavailable.
hints: Begin with the subtopic conceptual processing order and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.

summary: Logical Processing of a Query is about making the database behavior and the expected result explicit.
Use the provided subtopics as a review checklist and validate a small test case.
Keep vendor-specific syntax, access assumptions, and production-safety boundaries visible.
